title: About
text:
This website was created for ISSS608: Visual Analytics & Applications.
Its purpose is to document and present the visualisations, analysis, and coursework outputs that I have completed throughout the module. The site acts as a structured portfolio of my work, allowing different exercises and assignments to be organised into separate sections for easy navigation.
The website was built using:

Quarto for website generation
RStudio for development
R for data visualisation and analysis
GitHub for version control
Vercel for deployment

Through this website, I aim to present my coursework in a clear, organised, and accessible format.

title: Hands-On Exercise 1
text:
This exercise looks to explore the fundamentals of visualisations with R.
pacman::p_load(tidyverse)

title: Hands-On Exercise 1
text:
geom_bar
Now let’s start with the easiest plot.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x=RACE)) +
  geom_bar()

title: Hands-On Exercise 1
text:
geom_dotplot

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot(dotsize = 0.5)

Bin width defaults to 1/30 of the range of the data. Pick better value with
`binwidth`.









Note: y scale is not very useful, in fact it is very misleading.
The following code below does 2 steps:

scale_y_continuous is used to turn off the y-axis, and
binwidth argument is used to change the binwidth to 2.5


ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth=2.5,         
               dotsize = 0.5) +      
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,           
                     breaks = NULL)

title: Hands-On Exercise 1
text:
geom_histogram()

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram()       

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.









It is to note that the default bin is 30.

Modifying a geometric object by changing geom()
The following code chunk does the following:

bins argument is used to change the number of bins to 20,
fill argument is used to shade the histogram with light blue color, and
color argument is used to change the outline colour of the bars in black


ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x= MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20,            
                 color="black",      
                 fill="light blue")  










Modifying a geometric object by changing aes()
The following code changes the fill of the histogram by using sub-group of `aesthetic()

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x= MATHS, 
           fill = GENDER)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="grey30")

title: Hands-On Exercise 1
text:
geom_density()
This computes and plots the kernel density estimate, which is a smoothed version of the histogram.
It is a useflu alternative to the histogram for continuous data that comes from an underlying smooth distribution.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_density()








The next code plots 2 kernel density lines by using colour or fill arguments of aes()

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, 
           colour = GENDER)) +
  geom_density()

title: Hands-On Exercise 1
text:
geom_boxplot()

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS,       
           x= GENDER)) +    
  geom_boxplot()            








Notches are used in boxplots to help visually assess whether medians of distributions differ. If it does not overlap, it means that the medians are different.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS, 
           x= GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot(notch=TRUE)

title: Hands-On Exercise 1
section: Adding best-fit curve on a scatterplot
text:
Adding best-fit curve on a scatterplot
The code below shows geom_smooth() being used to plot a best-fit curve in the scatterplot. The default method used is loess

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x= MATHS, y=ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(size=0.5)

Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.


`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









The default smoothing method can be overridden as shown below.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x= MATHS, 
           y=ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method=lm, 
              linewidth=0.5)

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

title: Hands-On Exercise 1
text:
facet_wrap()
This code wraps a 1-D sequence of panels into 2-D. This is generally a better use of screen space than facet_grid because most displays are roughly rectangular.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x= MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20) +
    facet_wrap(~ CLASS)

title: Hands-On Exercise 1
text:
facet_grid()
This code forms a matrix of panels defined by row and column facetting variables. It is most useful when you have two discrete variables, and all combinations of the variables exist in the data.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x= MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20) +
    facet_grid(~ CLASS)

title: Hands-On Exercise 1
section: Changing the range of x & y-axis
text:
Changing the range of x & y-axis
As the scatterplot below is slightly misleading due to the axis range not being equal,

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x= MATHS, y=ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method=lm, size=0.5)

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









the code below fixes both axis range from 0 to 100.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x= MATHS, y=ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method=lm, 
              size=0.5) +  
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100),
                  ylim=c(0,100))

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

title: Hands-On Exercise 2
text:
This exercise builds on what was covered in Hands-On Exercise 1, where we explore more extensions of ggplot2 extensions that will allow the creation of a more elegant and effective statistical graphics.
In this exercise, 4 R packages will be used:

pacman::p_load(ggrepel, patchwork, 
               ggthemes, hrbrthemes,

exam_data <- read_csv("../data/Exam_data.csv")

title: Hands-On Exercise 2
text:
How does ggrepel work?
The code block below shows the implementation of ggrepel based on the scatter plot that was done above.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x= MATHS, 
           y=ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method=lm, 
              size=0.5) +  
  geom_label_repel(aes(label = ID), 
                   fontface = "bold") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100),
                  ylim=c(0,100)) +
  ggtitle("English scores versus Maths scores for Primary 3")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

title: Hands-On Exercise 2
text:
How would ggtheme package work?
With the above example given, let’s explore the package. This pacakage provides themes that would replicate looks of plot by Edward Tufte, Stephen Few, Fivethirtyeight, The Economist, ‘Stata’, ‘Excel’, and The Wall Street Journal, among others.
The following code example below follows the Economist theme is used.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
             aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 boundary = 100,
                 color="grey25", 
                 fill="grey90") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths scores") +
  theme_economist()

title: Hands-On Exercise 2
text:
How does hrbthemes work?
Using the example given above, the code block below does 3 changes:

axis_title_size argument is used to increase the font size to 18
base_size argument is used to increase the default axis label to 15
grid argument is used to remove the x-axis grid lines

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
             aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 boundary = 100,
                 color="grey25", 
                 fill="grey90") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths scores") +
  theme_ipsum(axis_title_size = 18,
              base_size = 15,
              grid = "Y")

title: Hands-On Exercise 2
section: Using the patchwork extension to create composite graphics
text:
Using the patchwork extension to create composite graphics
This extension is one of the ggplot2 extensions which is designed to combine separate ggplot2 graphs into single figure.
The general syntax that combines graphs are as follows:

2-column layout using the + sign
() to create a subplot group
2-row layout using the / sign


2 graphs combined
The code block below shows how 2 histograms are combined

p1 + p2










3 graphs combined
The code block below does the following to combine 3 plots:

/ stacks 2 ggplot2 graphs
| places the plots beside each other
() defines the sequence of the plotting


(p1 / p2) | p3

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'











Creating the composite figure with tags
The package also provides auto-tagging capabilities to identify the subplots in the figure with plot_annotation().

((p1 / p2) | p3) + 
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = 'I')

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'











Creating the composite figure with insert
The package also allows plots to be placed freely on top/below another plot with inset_element().

p3 + inset_element(p2, 
                   left = 0.02, 
                   bottom = 0.7, 
                   right = 0.5, 
                   top = 1)

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'











Combining both patchwork and ggtheme while creating a composite figure
The code block showcases how both ggtheme and patchwork can be combined.

patchwork <- (p1 / p2) | p3
patchwork & theme_economist()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

title: Hands-On Exercise 3
text:
The tooltip aesthetic
The following code chunks below plots the interactive statistical graph using the ggiraph pacakge. This performs the following:

ggplot() object is first created. along with geom_dotplot_interactive() where it generates an interactive version of the graph
girafe() is used to generate an svg object to be displayed on an html page


Tooltip with only Student’s ID

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = ID),
    stackgroups = TRUE, 
    binwidth = 1, 
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, 
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 6,
  height_svg = 6*0.618
)





When the mouse hovers over the points in the graph above, it will display the student’s ID. This is done by editing in the geom_dotplot_interactive() function, where aes(tooltip = ID).


Displaying multiple information using tooltip

exam_data$tooltip <- c(paste0(     
  "Name = ", exam_data$ID,         
  "\n Class = ", exam_data$CLASS)) 

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = exam_data$tooltip), 
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 8,
  height_svg = 8*0.618
)





In this code block, where both the student’s ID and the class the student is in are to be displayed, a variable exam_data$tooltip is created in the first 3 lines of code, where it defines how it will be displayed. Afterwards, in the main body of code, tooltip is then assigned to exam_data$tooltip.


Customise your tooltip style

tooltip_css <- "background-color:white; #<<
font-style:bold; color:black;" #<<

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(tooltip = ID),                   
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6*0.618,
  options = list(    #<<
    opts_tooltip(    #<<
      css = tooltip_css)) #<<
)                                        





In this code block, the style is changed, where the background colour is while and the font colour and black and bolded.
This is done by introducing the variable tooltip_css, where you will assign the background colour, font style and the colour.
Afterwards, within the girafe() function, there is an additional options, where you would reference the tooltip_css as such there.


Advanced tooltip: displaying statistics
Let’s say that I want to display the 90% confidence interval of the mean of each subjects in the graph below.

tooltip <- function(y, ymax, accuracy = .01) {
  mean <- scales::number(y, accuracy = accuracy)
  sem <- scales::number(ymax - y, accuracy = accuracy)
  paste("Mean maths scores:", mean, "+/-", sem)
}

gg_point <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
                   aes(x = RACE),
) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = MATHS, 
                   tooltip = after_stat(  
                     tooltip(y, ymax))),  
    fun.data = "mean_se", 
    geom = GeomInteractiveCol,  
    fill = "light blue"
  ) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = MATHS),
    fun.data = mean_se,
    geom = "errorbar", width = 0.2, size = 0.2
  )

Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.

girafe(ggobj = gg_point,
       width_svg = 8,
       height_svg = 8*0.618)





In the code chunk above, tooltip is referenced in the first 4 lines, where the function is created to calculate the mean scores for the subjects with the intervals, along with how it is going to be displayed.
After that, it is then pointed within stat_summary() as shown in the code chunk.

title: Hands-On Exercise 3
text:
The data_id aesthetic
Let’s say, I want to identify visually the students in the same class over the histodot graph below.

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(           
    aes(data_id = CLASS),             
    stackgroups = TRUE,               
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6*0.618                      
)                                        





What is done is that data_id is used within geom_dotplot_interactive() where it referenced CLASS (data_id = CLASS). As such, when the clicker hovers over the dots, the dots will change colour to orange, where it indicates the students that are in the same class. This allows me to visually see the distributions of the students.
It is to note that the default colour for this is orange, where: hover_css = "fill:orange;"

Re-styling the hover effect
Instead of the dot’s colour changing to orange, I would want to highlight the students that are in the same class.

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(data_id = CLASS),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6*0.618,
  options = list(                        
    opts_hover(css = "fill: #202020;"),  
    opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.2;") 
  )                                        
)                                        





In the code block above, options is introduced within the girafe() function, where you can do the highlighting effect as such.

title: Hands-On Exercise 3
section: Combine both tooltip and the hover effect
text:
Combine both tooltip and the hover effect
Now, I want to combine both effects on the statistical graph. The code chunk below shows how it is done.

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(tooltip = CLASS, 
        data_id = CLASS),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6*0.618,
  options = list(                        
    opts_hover(css = "fill: #202020;"),  
    opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.2;") 
  )                                        
)                                        





The graph shows how the students in the same class is both highlighted, and shown as the tooltip.

title: Hands-On Exercise 3
text:
The onclick effect
This argument provides a way where upon the click of an data point, it leads you to another webpage.
This code chunk shows an example of the use of the argument, where exam_data$onclick is introduced in the first 3 lines.

exam_data$onclick <- sprintf("window.open(\"%s%s\")",
"https://www.moe.gov.sg/schoolfinder?journey=Primary%20school",
as.character(exam_data$ID))

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(onclick = onclick),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6*0.618)

title: Hands-On Exercise 3
text:
Coordinated Multiple Views
In hands-on exercise 2, we came across the use of multiple graphs. This can also be applied in interactive statistical graphs as well.
In this example, I will be displaying the graph of marks for both Maths and Science. When the mouse hovers over a data point in either graph, the corresponding data point on the other visualisation will be highlighted as well.
This is done by:

Using appropriate interactive functions of ggiraph to create the multiple views.
Using patchwork function within the girafe function to create the interactive coordinated multiple views.

The code chunk below showcases that.

p1 <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(data_id = ID),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +  
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100)) + 
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)

p2 <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(data_id = ID),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") + 
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100)) + 
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)

girafe(code = print(p1 + p2), 
       width_svg = 6,
       height_svg = 3,
       options = list(
         opts_hover(css = "fill: #202020;"),
         opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.2;")
         )
       ) 





The data_id aesthetic is critical to link observations between both plots, while the tooltip aesthetic is optional but a nice to have to improve the visualisation.

title: Hands-On Exercise 3
text:
Coordinated Multiple Views with plotly
To create a coordinated linked plot using plotly, 3 steps need to be done:

highlight_key() of plotly is used as shared data
2 scatterplots will be created using ggplot2 functions
`subplot() of plotly is used to place them next to each other side-by-side


d <- highlight_key(exam_data)
p1 <- ggplot(data=d, 
            aes(x = MATHS,
                y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(size=1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100),
                  ylim=c(0,100))

p2 <- ggplot(data=d, 
            aes(x = MATHS,
                y = SCIENCE)) +
  geom_point(size=1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100),
                  ylim=c(0,100))
subplot(ggplotly(p1),
        ggplotly(p2))





It is to note that highlight_key() simply creates an object of class crosstalk::SharedData.

title: Hands-On Exercise 3
text:
The Data Table, aka DT
This is a wrapper of the JavaScript Library DataTables.
Data objects in R can be rendered as HTML tables using this library.

DT::datatable(exam_data, class= "compact")

title: Hands-On Exercise 3
text:
The crosstalk method - Linked Brushing
The following code chunk below implements the coordinated brushing.

d <- highlight_key(exam_data) 
p <- ggplot(d, 
            aes(ENGLISH, 
                MATHS)) + 
  geom_point(size=1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100),
                  ylim=c(0,100))

gg <- highlight(ggplotly(p),        
                "plotly_selected")  

crosstalk::bscols(gg,               
                  DT::datatable(d), 
                  widths = 5)        

Setting the `off` event (i.e., 'plotly_deselect') to match the `on` event (i.e., 'plotly_selected'). You can change this default via the `highlight()` function.
















The highlight() is a function of the plotly package, where it sets a variety of options for brushing (basically highlighting) multiple plots. It is primarily designed for linking multiple plotly graphs, and it may not behave as expected when linking plotly to another htmlwidget package via crosstalk.
The bscols() is a helper function of crosstalk package, where it makes it easy to input HTML elements side by side. It can be called directly from the console but it is especially designed to work in a R markdown document. WARNING: This will bring in all of Bootstrap!

title: Hands-On Exercise 3
text:
Importing the dataset
First, the code chunk below imports the data GlobalPopulation where it will be used for this exercise.

col <- c("Country", "Continent")
globalPop <- read_xls("../data/GlobalPopulation.xls",
                      sheet="Data") %>%
  mutate(across(col, as.factor)) %>%
  mutate(Year = as.integer(Year))

title: Hands-On Exercise 3
text:
gganimate - The ANImethod Data Visualisation
This extends the grammar of graphics as implemented by ggplot2 to include the description of animation. It does this by providing a range of new grammar classes that can be added to the plot object in order to customise how it should change with time.
The functions are as shown below:

transition_*(): how the data should be spread out and how it relates to itself across time
view_*(): how the positional scales should change along the animation
shadow_*()`: how data from other points in time should be presented in the given point in time
enter_*()/exit_*(): how new data should appear and how old data should disappear during the course of the animation
ease_aes(): how different aesthetics should be eased during transitions


Creating a static population bubble plot
The code chunk below creates a static bubble plot:

ggplot(globalPop, aes(x = Old, y = Young, 
                      size = Population, 
                      colour = Country)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, 
             show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 12)) +
  labs(title = 'Year: {frame_time}', 
       x = '% Aged', 
       y = '% Young') 










Building it up to be animated
The following code chunk does the following:

transition_time() of gganimate will be used to create the transition through distinct states in time, which in this case, its year.
ease_aes() is used to control easing of aesthetics. By default, it is linear. Other methods include quadratic, cubic, quartic, quintic, sine, circular, exponential, elastic, back, and bounce.


ggplot(globalPop, aes(x = Old, y = Young, 
                      size = Population, 
                      colour = Country)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, 
             show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 12)) +
  labs(title = 'Year: {frame_time}', 
       x = '% Aged', 
       y = '% Young') +
  transition_time(Year) +       
  ease_aes('linear')

title: Hands-On Exercise 3
section: plotly - The Other ANImethod of Data Visualisation
text:
plotly - The Other ANImethod of Data Visualisation
In this package, both ggplotly() and plot_ly() support key frame animations through the frame argument/aethetics. They also support an ids argument/aesthetic to ensure smooth transitions between objects with the same id (which helps facilitate object constancy).

Building the animation with ggplotly()
In the code block below, the following is done:

Appropriate ggplot2 functions are used to create a static bubble plot. The output is then saved as an R object called gg.
ggplotly() is then used to convert the R graphic object into an animated svg object

In this example, if I want to not display the legend, the following would be used: show.legend = FALSE. However, theme(legend.position='none') is used, as the legend would still appear if the previous argument was used.

gg <- ggplot(globalPop, 
       aes(x = Old, 
           y = Young, 
           size = Population, 
           colour = Country)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = Population,
                 frame = Year),
             alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 12)) +
  labs(x = '% Aged', 
       y = '% Young') + 
  theme(legend.position='none')

Warning in geom_point(aes(size = Population, frame = Year), alpha = 0.7):
Ignoring unknown aesthetics: frame

ggplotly(gg)

Warning in p$x$data[firstFrame] <- p$x$frames[[1]]$data: number of items to
replace is not a multiple of replacement length








Building the animation with plot_ly()
The code chunk below shows how plot_ly() is utilised to animate the bubble plot.

bp <- globalPop %>%
  plot_ly(x = ~Old, 
          y = ~Young, 
          size = ~Population, 
          color = ~Continent,
          sizes = c(2, 100),
          frame = ~Year, 
          text = ~Country, 
          hoverinfo = "text",
          type = 'scatter',
          mode = 'markers'
          ) %>%
  layout(showlegend = FALSE)
bp

title: Hands-On Exercise 2
text:
How does ggrepel work?
The code block below shows the implementation of ggrepel based on the scatter plot that was done above.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x= MATHS, 
           y=ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method=lm, 
              size=0.5) +  
  geom_label_repel(aes(label = ID), 
                   fontface = "bold") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100),
                  ylim=c(0,100)) +
  ggtitle("English scores versus Maths scores for Primary 3")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

title: Hands-On Exercise 2
text:
How would ggtheme package work?
With the above example given, let’s explore the package. This pacakage provides themes that would replicate looks of plot by Edward Tufte, Stephen Few, Fivethirtyeight, The Economist, ‘Stata’, ‘Excel’, and The Wall Street Journal, among others.
The following code example below follows the Economist theme is used.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
             aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 boundary = 100,
                 color="grey25", 
                 fill="grey90") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths scores") +
  theme_economist()

title: Hands-On Exercise 2
text:
How does hrbthemes work?
Using the example given above, the code block below does 3 changes:

axis_title_size argument is used to increase the font size to 18
base_size argument is used to increase the default axis label to 15
grid argument is used to remove the x-axis grid lines

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
             aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 boundary = 100,
                 color="grey25", 
                 fill="grey90") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths scores") +
  theme_ipsum(axis_title_size = 18,
              base_size = 15,
              grid = "Y")

title: Hands-On Exercise 2
section: Using the patchwork extension to create composite graphics
text:
Using the patchwork extension to create composite graphics
This extension is one of the ggplot2 extensions which is designed to combine separate ggplot2 graphs into single figure.
The general syntax that combines graphs are as follows:

2-column layout using the + sign
() to create a subplot group
2-row layout using the / sign


2 graphs combined
The code block below shows how 2 histograms are combined

p1 + p2










3 graphs combined
The code block below does the following to combine 3 plots:

/ stacks 2 ggplot2 graphs
| places the plots beside each other
() defines the sequence of the plotting


(p1 / p2) | p3

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'











Creating the composite figure with tags
The package also provides auto-tagging capabilities to identify the subplots in the figure with plot_annotation().

((p1 / p2) | p3) + 
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = 'I')

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'











Creating the composite figure with insert
The package also allows plots to be placed freely on top/below another plot with inset_element().

p3 + inset_element(p2, 
                   left = 0.02, 
                   bottom = 0.7, 
                   right = 0.5, 
                   top = 1)

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'











Combining both patchwork and ggtheme while creating a composite figure
The code block showcases how both ggtheme and patchwork can be combined.

patchwork <- (p1 / p2) | p3
patchwork & theme_economist()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'
